ncert.chapter_hint: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

notes: 11 Objective I items rebuilt, plus de Broglie items to cover the chapter's second half. The photon-momentum family (items 2, 3, 5) is kept together, since the contrast between $ E \propto 1/\lambda $ and $ p \propto 1/\lambda $ is the point.

practice_bank.title: Practice — Photoelectric Effect and Wave-Particle Duality
practice_bank.intro: Eleven questions on photons and matter waves. The decisive fact about the photoelectric effect: it depends on the *frequency* of the light, not its brightness.

sections.title: Photons: Energy and Momentum
sections.blurb: Both go as 1/λ, but they are not the same quantity.

items.prompt: The Planck constant has the same dimensions as
items.explanation: From $ E = h\nu $, $ h $ is energy × time — and energy is force × distance, so $ h $ has the dimensions of force × distance × time. That combination is also angular momentum, which is why $ h $ appears wherever angular momentum is quantised.

options: of equal wavelength have equal linear momenta
of equal energy have unequal momenta
of equal frequency have unequal momenta
of equal momenta have unequal wavelengths
items.explanation: For a photon $ p = h/\lambda $, so wavelength alone fixes the momentum. And since $ E = hc/\lambda $ too, equal energy, equal frequency and equal wavelength all imply equal momentum for photons — the three are inseparable here, unlike for particles with mass.

items.prompt: If a photon's wavelength is decreased, its momentum $ p $ and energy $ E $
items.explanation: Both $ p = h/\lambda $ and $ E = hc/\lambda $ vary inversely with wavelength, so shortening it raises both together. This is why gamma rays, with the shortest wavelengths, are both the most energetic and the most penetrating radiation.

items.prompt: The relation $ E = pc $ is valid
options: for an electron as well as a photon
for a photon but not an electron
for an electron but not a photon
items.explanation: The general relation is $ E^{2} = p^{2}c^{2} + m^{2}c^{4} $. A photon is massless, so it reduces to $ E = pc $. An electron has mass, so its rest energy contributes and $ E > pc $ always — at low speeds $ E \approx mc^{2} + p^{2}/2m $ instead.

items.prompt: A red bulb and a blue bulb of **equal power** emit $ n_r $ and $ n_b $ photons in a given time. Then
items.explanation: Red photons carry less energy each, since $ E = hc/\lambda $ and red has the longer wavelength. Delivering the same total power therefore requires *more* of them, so $ n_r > n_b $. Equal power means equal energy per second, not equal photons per second.

sections.title: The Photoelectric Effect
sections.blurb: A threshold in frequency, and nothing brightness can do about it.

items.prompt: A metal has work function $ h\nu_0 $. Light of frequency $ \nu $ falls on it. Photoemission occurs only if
items.explanation: Each photon delivers $ h\nu $ to a single electron, and freeing it costs at least $ h\nu_0 $. Below the threshold frequency no electron escapes however intense the light — because energy arrives in indivisible packets and two sub-threshold photons cannot combine their efforts.

items.prompt: Light of wavelength $ \lambda $ falls on a metal of work function $ hc/\lambda_0 $. Photoemission occurs only if
items.explanation: The condition $ \nu \ge \nu_0 $ becomes $ \lambda \le \lambda_0 $ when written in wavelengths, because frequency and wavelength are inversely related. The inequality *flips* — the single most common slip in this topic.

items.prompt: The intensity of light on a photoelectric cell is doubled, with the frequency unchanged. The **maximum kinetic energy** of the emitted electrons
items.explanation: Einstein's equation $ KE_{max} = h\nu - \phi $ contains no intensity term. Doubling the intensity doubles the *number* of photons and hence the photocurrent, but each photon still carries the same energy, so the electrons emerge with the same maximum energy. Classical wave theory predicted the opposite, and its failure here is what forced the photon picture.

items.prompt: The stopping potential in a photoelectric experiment depends on
options: the frequency of the incident light and the work function
the intensity of the light only
the intensity and the frequency equally
the area of the emitting surface
items.explanation: Stopping potential measures the maximum electron energy: $ eV_0 = h\nu - \phi $. It therefore rises linearly with frequency, with a slope $ h/e $ that is the same for every metal, and an intercept set by the work function. Intensity affects only how *many* electrons arrive, not how energetic they are.

sections.title: Matter Waves
sections.blurb: If light can behave as a particle, particles can behave as waves.

items.prompt: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of momentum $ p $ is
items.explanation: De Broglie's hypothesis extends the photon relation $ p = h/\lambda $ to all matter, giving $ \lambda = h/p $. Because $ h $ is so tiny, everyday objects have utterly unobservable wavelengths — but an electron's is comparable to atomic spacings, which is why electron diffraction is routine.

items.prompt: An electron and a proton have the same kinetic energy. Comparing their de Broglie wavelengths,
items.explanation: With $ p = \sqrt{2mKE} $, equal kinetic energy means the heavier particle has the larger momentum — and so the *shorter* wavelength. The much lighter electron therefore has the longer wavelength, by a factor of about $ \sqrt{1836} \approx 43 $.

worked_examples.label: Example 1 — Photon energy and momentum
worked_examples.problem: Find the energy (in joules and eV) and the momentum of a photon of wavelength $ 500 $ nm. Take $ h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} $ J s.
worked_examples.solution:
**Energy:**

$ E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{500 \times 10^{-9}} = \frac{1.989 \times 10^{-25}}{5 \times 10^{-7}} $

$ = 3.98 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J} $

**In electron-volts:**

$ E = \frac{3.98 \times 10^{-19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 2.48\ \text{eV} $

**Momentum:**

$ p = \frac{h}{\lambda} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{5 \times 10^{-7}} = 1.33 \times 10^{-27}\ \text{kg m s}^{-1} $

**A shortcut worth memorising.** $ E(\text{eV}) = \frac{1240}{\lambda(\text{nm})} $. For $ 500 $ nm that gives $ 2.48 $ eV instantly, and it makes the whole visible spectrum easy: $ 400 $ nm is $ 3.1 $ eV, $ 700 $ nm is $ 1.77 $ eV.

**Why visible-light energies matter.** At $ 1.8$–$3.1 $ eV, visible photons are just energetic enough to trigger chemical changes — in the retina, in photosynthesis, in photographic film. Infrared photons are too feeble; ultraviolet ones are energetic enough to break bonds, which is why they cause sunburn.

worked_examples.label: Example 2 — Einstein's photoelectric equation
worked_examples.problem: Light of wavelength $ 400 $ nm falls on a metal of work function $ 2.0 $ eV. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons and the stopping potential.
worked_examples.solution:
**Photon energy**, using the shortcut:

$ E = \frac{1240}{400} = 3.1\ \text{eV} $

**Maximum kinetic energy:**

$ KE_{max} = h\nu - \phi = 3.1 - 2.0 = 1.1\ \text{eV} $

**Stopping potential.** Since $ eV_0 = KE_{max} $ and the energy is already in eV:

$ V_0 = 1.1\ \text{V} $

**Threshold wavelength for this metal:**

$ \lambda_0 = \frac{1240}{2.0} = 620\ \text{nm} $

So any light with $ \lambda < 620 $ nm will eject electrons — this metal responds to blue and green but not to red.

**Why working in eV is worth the habit.** The stopping potential in volts equals the maximum kinetic energy in eV numerically, so no conversion is needed at all. Working in joules means dividing by $ e $ at the end and inviting an arithmetic slip.

worked_examples.label: Example 3 — Threshold frequency and work function
worked_examples.problem: The stopping potential for a metal is $ 1.2 $ V at $ 350 $ nm and $ 0.4 $ V at $ 450 $ nm. Find the work function and Planck's constant.
worked_examples.solution:
**Set up the two equations.** With $ E = 1240/\lambda $ in eV:

At $ 350 $ nm: $ \frac{1240}{350} = 3.543 $ eV, so $ 3.543 = \phi + 1.2 $

At $ 450 $ nm: $ \frac{1240}{450} = 2.756 $ eV, so $ 2.756 = \phi + 0.4 $

**Both give:**

$ \phi = 2.34\ \text{eV} $ and $ \phi = 2.36\ \text{eV} $ — agreeing to within rounding, so $ \phi \approx 2.35 $ eV.

**Planck's constant from the slope.** Using the two frequencies:

$ \nu_1 = \frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{350 \times 10^{-9}} = 8.57 \times 10^{14} $ Hz, $ \nu_2 = 6.67 \times 10^{14} $ Hz

$ h = \frac{e(V_1 - V_2)}{\nu_1 - \nu_2} = \frac{(1.6 \times 10^{-19})(0.8)}{1.90 \times 10^{14}} = 6.74 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s} $

**Why this experiment mattered so much.** The graph of stopping potential against frequency is a straight line whose slope is $ h/e $ — *the same for every metal*, with only the intercept changing. Millikan's careful confirmation of that universality is what secured Einstein's photon hypothesis and, eventually, his Nobel Prize.

worked_examples.label: Example 4 — Intensity versus frequency
worked_examples.problem: A photoelectric cell is illuminated by $ 300 $ nm light. State what happens to the photocurrent and to the stopping potential if (a) the intensity is doubled and (b) the wavelength is changed to $ 250 $ nm at the same intensity.
worked_examples.solution:
**(a) Intensity doubled, wavelength unchanged.**

Photocurrent: **doubles**. Twice as many photons arrive, so twice as many electrons are ejected.

Stopping potential: **unchanged**. Each photon still carries $ 1240/300 = 4.13 $ eV, so the maximum electron energy is the same.

**(b) Wavelength shortened to $ 250 $ nm, intensity unchanged.**

Photon energy rises to $ 1240/250 = 4.96 $ eV, so the stopping potential **increases** by $ 4.96 - 4.13 = 0.83 $ V.

Photocurrent: **decreases slightly**. Same intensity means the same energy per second, but each photon now carries more of it — so *fewer* photons arrive, and fewer electrons are ejected.

**The two independent controls.** Intensity governs the *number* of electrons; frequency governs their *energy*. No amount of intensity can push electrons past the energy that frequency allows, and it is precisely this separation that classical wave theory could not explain.

worked_examples.label: Example 5 — de Broglie wavelength of an electron
worked_examples.problem: Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through $ 100 $ V.
worked_examples.solution:
**Momentum from the accelerating voltage:**

$ eV = \frac{p^{2}}{2m} \Rightarrow p = \sqrt{2meV} $

$ = \sqrt{2(9.1 \times 10^{-31})(1.6 \times 10^{-19})(100)} $

$ = \sqrt{2.912 \times 10^{-47}} = 5.40 \times 10^{-24}\ \text{kg m s}^{-1} $

**Wavelength:**

$ \lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{5.40 \times 10^{-24}} = 1.23 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m} = 0.123\ \text{nm} $

**A shortcut worth carrying:** $ \lambda(\text{nm}) = \frac{1.23}{\sqrt{V}} $ for electrons. At $ 100 $ V that gives $ 0.123 $ nm immediately.

**Why this number is so significant.** It is comparable to atomic spacings in crystals, which is exactly why electrons diffract from crystal lattices — as Davisson and Germer found in 1927, confirming de Broglie's hypothesis.

**And why electron microscopes beat optical ones.** Resolution scales with wavelength, and $ 0.123 $ nm is some four thousand times shorter than visible light. Raising the accelerating voltage shortens it further still.

worked_examples.label: Example 6 — Comparing photon and electron wavelengths
worked_examples.problem: A photon and an electron both have energy $ 100 $ eV. Compare their de Broglie wavelengths.
worked_examples.solution:
**The photon.** For a massless particle $ E = pc $, so

$ \lambda = \frac{hc}{E} = \frac{1240}{100} = 12.4\ \text{nm} $

**The electron.** Here $ E = p^{2}/2m $, so $ p = \sqrt{2mE} $ and, from the previous shortcut,

$ \lambda = \frac{1.23}{\sqrt{100}} = 0.123\ \text{nm} $

**Ratio:** the photon's wavelength is about **100 times longer**.

**Why the difference is so large.** For the photon $ \lambda \propto 1/E $; for the non-relativistic electron $ \lambda \propto 1/\sqrt{E} $. The electron's rest mass gives it far more momentum for the same kinetic energy, and momentum is what sets the wavelength.

**The practical consequence.** At the same energy, electrons probe far finer detail than photons — which is the whole reason electron microscopy exists. To match an electron's $ 0.123 $ nm, a photon would need about $ 10 $ keV, putting it in the X-ray region.

worked_examples.label: Example 7 — Number of photons and photocurrent
worked_examples.problem: A photocell receives $ 1.5 $ mW of $ 400 $ nm light. If $ 5\% $ of the incident photons eject an electron, find the photocurrent.
worked_examples.solution:
**Photon energy:**

$ E = \frac{1240}{400} = 3.1\ \text{eV} = (3.1)(1.6 \times 10^{-19}) = 4.96 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J} $

**Photons per second:**

$ n = \frac{P}{E} = \frac{1.5 \times 10^{-3}}{4.96 \times 10^{-19}} = 3.02 \times 10^{15}\ \text{s}^{-1} $

**Electrons per second**, at $ 5\% $ efficiency:

$ n_e = (0.05)(3.02 \times 10^{15}) = 1.51 \times 10^{14}\ \text{s}^{-1} $

**Photocurrent:**

$ i = n_e e = (1.51 \times 10^{14})(1.6 \times 10^{-19}) = 2.42 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{A} = 24.2\ \mu\text{A} $

**What the quantum efficiency represents.** Most photons are reflected, absorbed without ejecting an electron, or eject one that fails to escape the surface. Real photocathodes manage $ 5$–$30\% $; modern silicon photodiodes exceed $ 80\% $.

**Why the current is proportional to intensity.** Doubling the light doubles the photons, hence the electrons, hence the current — which is exactly what makes a photocell a usable light meter.

worked_examples.label: Example 8 — Why the wave theory failed
worked_examples.problem: Estimate the time a classical wave theory would predict for a $ 1\ \mu\text{W m}^{-2} $ beam to supply $ 2 $ eV to an electron in an atom of radius $ 10^{-10} $ m, and contrast with observation.
worked_examples.solution:
**Power intercepted by one atom.** Taking its cross-section as $ \pi r^{2} $:

$ A = \pi(10^{-10})^{2} = 3.14 \times 10^{-20}\ \text{m}^{2} $

$ P = (10^{-6})(3.14 \times 10^{-20}) = 3.14 \times 10^{-26}\ \text{W} $

**Energy needed:**

$ E = 2\ \text{eV} = 3.2 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J} $

**Time required on the classical picture:**

$ t = \frac{E}{P} = \frac{3.2 \times 10^{-19}}{3.14 \times 10^{-26}} = 1.0 \times 10^{7}\ \text{s} $

About **four months**.

**What is actually observed.** Photoemission begins within $ 10^{-9} $ s of the light arriving — sixteen orders of magnitude sooner.

**Why the photon picture resolves it.** Energy does not trickle in as a spread-out wave; it arrives in whole packets of $ h\nu $, one of which can be absorbed by a single electron instantly. Together with the frequency threshold and the intensity-independence of $ KE_{max} $, this timing argument is the third independent reason the classical wave theory of light had to be supplemented.
